name: Lavender Blue
lede: Lavender Blue is a pale, slightly violet blue named for the flower, and an old entry in the systems naturalists used to describe butterflies, flowers and stones.

sections.title: A flower and a dictionary entry
sections.body:
Paterson defines lavender as a pale lilac and lists lavender grey and lavender blue as relatives [1]. He suggests the flower's name may come from the Latin *lavare*, to wash [1]. His entry for China blue is simply a lavender blue [1].

The pair of words is older than the paint chips. Baty prints a family of the older naturalists' color lists, and several of them already carry a Lavender-blue among the blues, next to Smalt-blue and Violet-blue [2]. In Werner's tradition the same hue sits under purple, where Baty explains that Lavender Purple is Werner's lavender blue, mixed from blue and red with a little brown and grey [3]. The examples are dried lavender flowers, the light spots of the peacock butterfly and a porcelain jasper [3]. See also [[flower:lavender|lavender]] itself, and [[lavender-grey]].

sections.title: Which lavender blue
sections.body: The library carries several, and they are not close. The swatch here, a pale violet-tinged blue, is listed with ISCC-NBS blocks 195 and 198, with Maerz and Paul's first recorded use in 1796 and with Ridgway's 1912 plate XXIII [4]. Ridgway's scanned plate is an aged, approximate swatch, ΔE 2.4 from the entry Pallid Soft Blue-Violet [4]. A separate, much stronger lavender blue also exists, #8B88F8, from an online survey [4]. The nearest everyday name is [[periwinkle]], 10.3 units away [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Only 3 of 23,781 archive paintings carry a color within six units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas [5]. They are all light in tone, with two in three sitting in the highlight range [5]. Adam Pynacker's [[painting:commons-Q65972069|Tower on a Coast]] of 1660 holds it across 25 per cent, and the earliest, Claude Lorrain's [[painting:commons-Q114241452|landscape with dancing peasants]] of 1637, holds it across 11 per cent [5]. Both are probably sky. With only three paintings, none of this proves a pattern [5].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a match is a screen color, not a pigment [5].
